To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a panel of monoclonal antibodies can be used to phenotype solid tumors; 2) the phenotyping is useful for devising biotherapies; and 3) a ‘cocktail’ approach is useful in devising patient-specific immunoconjugate therapy.

a panel of 14 MoAbs (4 raised against human breast cancer, 4 against human colon cancer and 6 against melanoma) was used to phenotype frozen tissue sections of human solid tumors obtained from 110 cancer patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of patient- or tumor-type-specific therapeutic immunoagents, and the use of monoclonal antibodies to identify the appropriate targets.
the development of biotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of human solid tumors, based on monoclonal antibody technology.
devising biotherapies that will be effective against metastatic cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MoAbs have a limited role in the treatment of human cancer, at least in their present state of development.

1. the MoAbs we have raised are useful tools for tumor immunophenotyping; 2. they have potential as reagents for the development of biotherapeutic immunoconjugate strategies; and 3. they can be used for the development of diagnostic immunoassays.

the MoAbs we have developed and used for the characterization of human tumors are useful for the selection of a patient-specific cocktail of MoAbs, and that the cocktail of MoAb can be further modified by the use of MoAbs that recognize the antigens expressed on tumor cells, but not on normal tissue cells, in order to minimize the toxicity of immunotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified 9 monoclonal antibodies that bind to 6 tumor antigens that are expressed on 100% of breast, colon and melanoma tumors.
we have been able to identify MoAbs that are specific for breast cancer cells, colon cancer cells and melanoma cells.
we are able to identify a panel of MoAbs which can be used to immunophenotype the tumor of a given individual.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the immunophenotype of a tumor can vary from one patient to another, and from one lesion of the same patient to another, so that it is important to analyze each tumor individually in order to devise the best therapeutic approach.
the heterogeneity of the expression of tumor-associated antigens in human solid tumors is such that a single MoAb is not likely to react with all the tumor cells in a single patient.
it is possible to devise patient-specific biotherapeutic strategies by immunophenotyping the tumor lesions of individual patients.
